# 2 Samuel 22:27–51: Research notes

## Background for the whole passage
- This song is almost word for word the same as Psalm 18. Boice (quoted by Guzik) calls it close to David's final words, a thank-you summary for a lifetime of rescues. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- Constable notes it is one of the oldest major poems in the Old Testament. Because it closely matches Psalm 18, it is a key passage for comparing ancient copies of the text. He shares out the chapter's sections, with vv. 31–51 as "the Lord's excellence." He also says the song begins with "The LORD" and ends with "forever." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html
- The NET Bible's opening note says the song shows that God vindicates those who are blameless and loyal, and keeps his promises by giving the king victory and power over nations. https://bible.org/netbible/2sa22_notes.htm
- William Kelly reads David as a type (foreshadowing) of Christ throughout Samuel, and David's enemies as pictures of antichrists. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/22-27.html

## Verse by verse

**v. 27**
- Keil & Delitzsch: vv. 26–27 turn the reason for David's rescue into a general rule. God treats people according to how they treat him. The Hebrew builds God's verbs from the same words used for the people's conduct. God "shows himself crooked" to the perverse by handing them over to their own perverseness (Romans 1:28). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-27.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/2-samuel/22-27.html
- Another note on the same Biblehub page says "unsavoury" is better translated "perverse." It means God leaves the twisted person to follow his own twistedness until it destroys him (compare Balaam). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-27.htm
- Guzik says translators struggle with this line. He quotes Boice: the Hebrew root means "twisted," so the line literally says God shows himself twisted to the twisted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- Constable: God is "shrewd" to the crooked in that he turns them into fools. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html
- Biblehub's study notes: God's shrewdness is not deceit. It shows his justice, and he cannot be fooled. The notes link the first half to Matthew 5:8 ("pure in heart") and the second to God using wicked schemes for good, as with Joseph (Genesis 50:20). https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/22-27.htm
- Lange/Erdmann: God's justice shows up according to where a person stands with him. The translator adds that the point is simply that God does evil to the person who does evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/2_samuel/22.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: if people deal plainly with God, he deals plainly with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-samuel-22.html
- Hawker: a believer values God's righteousness as much as his mercy, because both meet in Jesus (Titus 1:15). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/2-samuel/22-27.html

**v. 28**
- Keil & Delitzsch: this applies the general rule to God's people. The "afflicted people" are the godly, downtrodden ones in the nation. The "haughty" are the godless rich and powerful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-27.htm
- Guzik ties it to the principle that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- Lange: v. 28 backs up vv. 26–27 by pointing to how God actually treats the humble and the proud. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/2_samuel/22.htm

**v. 29**
- Guzik: when God met David's need, he brought light first, because strength and skill are little use if you can't see. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says light stands for well-being, and a burning lamp for a lasting source of joy and strength. A homily on the same page adds that even "children of the day" sometimes need candlelight, and the flame comes from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-samuel-22.html
- Spurgeon wrote a Faith's Checkbook devotional on this verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2samuel

**v. 30**
- Guzik: God gave strength; one man shouldn't be able to take on a troop. He sees the principle of Ephesians 6:10 here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- NET: "with your help I can charge against an army." The word for army is more exactly a raiding party or group of troops. The KJV margin has "broken" for "run." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=2Sa&chapter=22&verse=30

**v. 31**
- Guzik: God also brought protection. Trust was the vital link to receiving it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- Precept Austin: having come through the fire, David could say God's word, including the promise of the throne, had survived. Not one promise had burned away (compare Joshua's "not one good promise failed"). https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary
- Pulpit Commentary: God's word "cannot change" and has been tested countless times. Seeing how perfect it is takes personal experience. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-22.html

**v. 32**
- NET translates "Rock" as "protector." The rocky-cliff image means protection. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=2Sa&chapter=22
- A Pulpit homily contrasts other refuges with God: they are limited, weak and short-lived, while he is unlimited, firm and everlasting. The excerpt doesn't say which verse it is about. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-22.html

**v. 33**
- NET: the Hebrew literally reads "sets free blameless his/my way." NET follows Psalm 18:32 ("made my path smooth"). The word *tamim* usually means morally blameless, but here it means a path clear of obstacles. https://bible.org/netbible/2sa22_notes.htm
- Some versions read "girds me with strength" (NAB, NJB). https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary
- Guzik's devotional on "He makes my way perfect": receive God's strength and rest in the promise, even while waiting or disappointed. https://enduringword.com/a-perfect-way/

**v. 34**
- Guzik: deer skip around without losing their footing. God gave David that kind of skill in facing his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- NET: "gives me the agility of a deer… negotiate the rugged terrain." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=2Sa&chapter=22

**v. 35**
- NET: David credits his skill with weapons to God. Egyptian carvings show gods teaching the king to shoot a bow. The "bronze bow" was probably strengthened with bronze strips, or was a ceremonial bow. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=2Sa&chapter=22&verse=35&tab=commentaries

**v. 36**
- **Text question.** Psalm 18:35 has "your gentleness/condescension." Samuel's Hebrew reads slightly differently. The Cambridge Bible and Keil & Delitzsch take it as "your answering/hearing," meaning God answers prayers for help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-36.htm
- NET agrees: "your willingness to help enables me to prevail" (literally "your answer makes me great"). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2Sa+22%3A1-51
- Guzik: it wasn't only skill and power. David also had a relationship with a God of great gentleness, and that too was a source of strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- Matthew Henry: God's grace and tender mercy made David great in wealth, authority and reputation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/22-36.html
- Spurgeon: we are so small that God's greatness without condescension would crush us, but he stoops to lift up the lowly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2samuel
- Expositor's Bible: David may be remembering how gently he handled weak lambs as a shepherd, a picture of how God treated him. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/2-samuel/22-36.html
- The Sermon Bible and Biblical Illustrator say Christ shows us this gentleness: "the light which shines from the Cross is the gentleness of God." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/2-samuel-22.html and https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/2-samuel-22.html
- Biblehub's study notes take the word to mean humility or meekness. Being lifted up comes from God's grace, not from ourselves (James 4:6, 10). https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/22-36.htm

**v. 37**
- Keil & Delitzsch: God widened David's steps by clearing obstacles out of his way, so his ankles held firm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-36.htm
- NET gives another option: "you widen my stride," meaning God lets him run fast. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2Sa+22%3A1-51

**vv. 38–43**
- NET renders vv. 38–42 as complete victory: "they cry out to the LORD, but he does not answer them." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2Sa+22%3A1-51
- v. 40, Preacher's Homiletical: "girded" pictures warriors tying up their clothes for hard effort. "Subdued" literally means "made to bow the knee." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-samuel-22.html
- Expositor's Bible raises the obvious question: how can David praise God's gentleness and then speak such terrible words about his enemies? The excerpt I saw didn't include the answer. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/2-samuel/22-36.html

**v. 44**
- Guzik: David had to deal with conflict from his own people as well as foreign enemies, and God carried him through that too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- NET: "strivings" probably has a military sense, and "people" may mean an army. "My" suggests attacks by David's own countrymen. https://bible.org/netbible/2sa22_notes.htm

**v. 45**
- NET: literally "at a report of an ear they submit." David's reputation is so great that people submit without a fight. https://bible.org/netbible/2sa22_notes.htm

**v. 46**
- NET: "lose heart" is literally "wither, wear out." https://bible.org/netbible/2sa22_notes.htm

**v. 47**
- NET: "The LORD lives" is normally an oath formula, but no oath follows here. It declares that God is present and acting, the living God, unlike pagan gods. The second "rock" may be an accidental repetition, since Psalm 18:46 doesn't have it. https://bible.org/netbible/2sa22_notes.htm and https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=2Sa&chapter=22
- Preacher's Homiletical: the phrase contrasts God with dead idols. Some modern interpreters see it as a coronation cheer ("Long live the king"), but Keil, Alexander and Erdmann say that would only fit a mortal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-samuel-22.html

**v. 48**
- Guzik: David is saying this was the LORD's victory, won for him, so the glory goes to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/

**v. 49**
- Guzik: David switches between speaking about God ("He delivers") and speaking to him ("You lift me up"). Both belong in praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- NET: "lift me up" probably means rescue, but it could mean "exalt," that is, make enemies recognise David's superiority. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=2Sa&chapter=22

**v. 50**
- Pulpit Commentary, quoting Erdmann: nations come to know God through the announcement of his great deeds, not the sword. David acts as a missionary here, and all missionary work is at bottom ongoing praise of God's name. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-22.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: God's grace to David was too great for its praise to stay within Israel's borders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-51.htm
- A devotional on Precept Austin: praise is the overflow of a joyful heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_devotionals

**v. 51**
- **Text question.** The traditional reading note (Qere) gives "tower of salvation," which is behind the KJV. The written text (Kethib), the ancient versions and Psalm 18:50 read "gives great deliverance." Keil & Delitzsch call the "tower" reading "a singular conjecture." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/22-51.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the king is not David alone but David's royal line, which reached its peak in Christ. The last line echoes the promise of 2 Samuel 7:12–16. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/2-samuel/22-51.html
- Matthew Henry: David rests on the promise in 2 Samuel 7, "with an eye to Christ," who alone is his seed forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/22-51.html
- Guzik: although David spoke of his own righteousness earlier, he ends by resting on God's mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/
- Constable and bible.org both note that Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:10) also ends with "his king" and "his anointed." Bible.org adds that, since the promise to David's dynasty, the whole line of kings is now the object of God's favour, finally fulfilled in the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/22-51.html and https://bible.org/seriespage/david%E2%80%99s-song-salvation-2-samuel-22
- Expositor's Bible: it's doubtful how far the whole psalm applies to Christ, but the closing words can surely be applied to David's Son. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/2-samuel/22-51.html
- Pulpit: "his anointed" is literally God's messiah (Christ). If David could have seen what we see, his gratitude would have had no limit. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_samuel/22-51.htm
- Ligonier (Reformed) frames v. 51 as God keeping his covenant with "steadfast love." It quotes Henry: God rewarded David "not of debt, but of grace." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/kindness-to-the-lords-anointed
- Translation note: some literal and Catholic translations bring out the word "anointed" directly. Smith's has "his Messiah," and the Catholic Public Domain Version has "David, his Christ." https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/22-51.htm

## What's missing
- **Differences between Protestant traditions:** none found. The sources I saw (Guzik, Henry, Spurgeon, Ligonier, Constable) agree on these verses.
- **Catholic, Orthodox, and prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace readings:** I reached none of those sites before the limit. The only "other view" I found is the coronation-cheer reading of v. 47, which comes second-hand through the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary.
- **To fill the gaps,** it would be worth checking the full Enduring Word, Gill and Pulpit pages directly, and searching newadvent.org/catholic.com and the Lutheran and Wesleyan sites. Two good searches would be Romans 15:9, which quotes v. 50 / Psalm 18:49, and Psalm 18 itself.
